q: What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient with acute kidney injury whose urinalysis reveals muddy brown granular casts?
A patient presents with acute kidney injury after taking amoxicillin. Urinalysis shows WBC casts and eosinophiluria. Diagnosis?

What do fatty casts (oval fat bodies, Maltese crosses under polarized light) indicate?
What do broad waxy casts indicate?
a: Chronic renal failure (they form in dilated, hypertrophied tubules)

q: What is the very first diagnostic step in a patient with unexplained new-onset Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)?
a: Renal ultrasound to rule out post-renal etiology (e.g., hydronephrosis/obstruction).

q: What BUN/Cr ratio and FENa+ are indicative of pre-renal azotemia?
a: BUN/Cr > 20:1 and FENa < 1% (kidneys are actively reabsorbing Na+ and water).

q: What are the absolute indications for urgent hemodialysis (AEIOU)?
a: Acidosis (severe, refractory), Electrolyte imbalance (severe hyperkalemia), Intoxication (Li, toxic alcohols, salicylates), Overload (refractory volume overload), Uremia (pericarditis, encephalopathy).

q: What is the first-line medication for a patient with severe hyperkalemia showing EKG changes (e.g., peaked T waves)?
a: IV Calcium Gluconate (or Calcium Chloride) to stabilize the cardiac myocyte membrane.

q: What is the best initial pharmacological prevention for recurrent calcium oxalate stones?
a: Thiazide diuretics (they increase renal calcium reabsorption, lowering urine calcium) and hydration. (Do NOT restrict dietary calcium).

q: What severe neurological complication occurs due to the rapid correction of hyponatremia?
a: Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome (Central Pontine Myelinolysis). "From low to high, your pons will die."

q: What severe complication occurs due to the rapid correction of hypernatremia?
a: Cerebral edema (Brain herniation). "From high to low, your brains will blow."

q: How do you differentiate between psychogenic polydipsia and central diabetes insipidus using a water deprivation test?
a: In psychogenic polydipsia, urine osmolality increases (concentrates) with water deprivation. In central DI, urine osmolality remains low (dilute) but increases significantly after administration of exogenous ADH (Desmopressin).

q: What is the diagnostic hallmark of Fibromuscular Dysplasia on renal angiography, typically seen in young women with resistant hypertension?
a: "String of beads" appearance of the renal arteries.

q: What is the preferred antihypertensive class for a patient with Scleroderma Renal Crisis?
a: ACE inhibitors (e.g., Captopril), even in the setting of acute kidney injury.

q: What ultrasound finding is highly characteristic of Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) in adults?
a: Bilateral, massively enlarged kidneys with numerous cysts. (Associated with berry aneurysms and hepatic cysts).

q: What is the classic pentad of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)?
a: FAT RN: Fever, Anemia (microangiopathic hemolytic), Thrombocytopenia, Renal failure, Neurologic symptoms. (Due to ADAMTS13 deficiency).

In the treatment of severe hypercalcemia, why are loop diuretics (like furosemide) no longer routinely recommended as first-line unless the patient is volume overloaded?
a: They can worsen volume depletion, which exacerbates hypercalcemia. Aggressive IV hydration with normal saline is the priority.

What typical EKG changes are associated with hypokalemia?
a: U waves, flattened/inverted T waves, and ST-segment depression.

q: In a patient with hypernatremia and hypovolemia, what is the best initial IV fluid to administer?
a: Isotonic Normal Saline (0.9% NaCl) to correct the volume deficit first, before switching to hypotonic fluids (like 5% Dextrose) to correct the free water deficit.
